b: Reflections on the passing of DBT creator Marsha Linehan, PhD.

Marsha Linehan, PhD, MA, died on November 10, 2026, at the age of 83. She was the most impactful woman in the history of psychology, and her dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) is among the best and most widely used treatments. Beyond professional achievements, Marsha's inspiring life served many therapists and patients as a model of self-healing and of giving back to others. After a turbulent adolescence as the ugly duckling of a highly successful family, Marsha spent 2 years in a dismal psychiatric hospital stay (much of it in seclusion); Marsha became her first and toughest patient. She turned around her own suffering and dedicated the rest of her life to helping others escape theirs.

Marsha's courageously frank autobiography, Building a Life Worth Living: A Memoir inspires hope for the hopeless and provides a path to recovery for those who are stuck in repetitive patterns of self-defeating behavior.1 Marsha was the essence of "the wounded healer," living proof that having severe psychiatric problems now doesn’t mean they'll last forever; that with suffering comes a wise mind and a deep heart; that helping others helps heal yourself; and to never give up, however hopeless the future may seem. Marsha's lived experience gave her the extraordinary wisdom and empathy that she displayed in all her clinical work, teaching, research, and writings.

Marsha's "dialectic" was to be the most validating of therapists, but also the most demanding. She provided radical acceptance for who you are now, but also expected you to put your heart and mind into learning the skills that would lead to positive change and a better life. She gave patients more than anyone I've known, but also expected them to work as hard as she did.
Marsha described the essentials of DBT in Cognitive-Behavioral Treatment of Borderline Personality Disorder, a classic book as useful and alive today as when it was written 35 years ago:2
Dialectics: finding a balance between acceptance & change
Mindfulness: staying grounded in the now
Distress tolerance via problem solving exercises
Emotional regulation to manage intense feelings
Interpersonal skills and setting healthy boundaries
Validation: meeting yourself realistically, but without self-directed aggression and harsh judgment.

An aside: Marsha accepted the book's title, which I suggested, only with great reluctance. She never liked the term "borderline personality disorder" and adopted it to describe her work only because it was necessary to get NIMH funding. And we didn't realize in those early days that "DBT" would become so popular in its own right that association with "CBT" wasn't unnecessary to legitimize it.

Marsha was among the most practical people I have ever met. She had a special gift for teaching simple techniques to help individuals cope with their complicated inner feelings and stressful life's dilemmas. She laid out for patients the 4 alternative ways patients deal with problems:
Solving them (changing themselves and/or their situations)
Feeling better about them (change their perceptions)
Marsha provided tools to achieve the first 3 options so as to help people avoid being trapped forever in the fourth.

Marsha’s most popular book DBT Skills Training Manual has sold more than 1.2 million copies. It is a goldmine of simple behavioral skills that help patients survive their very worst moments. To prevent self-harm cutting, she advised substituting a rubber band or feeling the sought for pain by immersing your arm in ice water. Self-destructive impulses can also be lessened and endured by physical or breathing exercises and muscle relaxation. When confronted with emotional or relational dilemmas, her advice is to stop, take a step back, observe, and proceed mindfully. She taught patients how to weigh consequences before acting dangerously.

Marsha was also a certified Zen master whose extensive training started in the 1980s and was renewed yearly by participating in and leading silent retreats. Drawing heavily from her own spiritual journey and her Roman Catholic roots, she translated ancient contemplative practices into practical, secular skills that patients can use to survive intense emotional pain. She used and taught "mindfulness"—an intense focus on the moment that leads to the harmonious blending of logic with feelings; a nonjudgmental awareness and radical acceptance of oneself and others, and a feeling of profound connectedness with life and the universe. Before working with Marsha, I advocated for what I mistakenly thought was a broad bio/psycho/social model of human nature and psychiatric treatment. She taught me that my model was far too narrow because it left out the 'spiritual' dimension of life—the human need to find meaning & hope. Marsha perfectly embodied and practiced a fully rounded, 4 dimensional biopsychosocial-spiritual model.

Looking back on my career, it's clear that its 2 most useful contributions were helping Marsha get her first NIMH grant and helping her write her first 2 books. I think of Marsha often and will miss her always. She was not just for our age, but for all time.
